source: Keppens (2026) An exploratory study of hybrid explanation of Bayesian network derived likelihood ratios
finding: GPT-5.4 given a full Bayesian network and asked to compute a likelihood ratio (LR) alone is often right but fails silently. Failures come in two forms: dropping a prior observation, and wrong propagation.
numbers: 100 repeated LR calculations per network, temperature 0.2. Four networks: example (correct 37.06), terpenes fire (1.006), cross-transfer (18.07), jury observation (0.662).
limits: Qualitative study, one model, four small networks, faithfulness only. Not a human comparison.
agent_relevance: Do not let the model compute LRs in its head. Compute them in code and hand the number to the model.

source: Keppens (2026) An exploratory study of hybrid explanation of Bayesian network derived likelihood ratios
finding: In the cross-transfer network the answer distribution was bimodal. The small wrong peak was the unconditioned LR of 390.4 instead of the correct 18.07. The model ignored the prior observation, then wrote a fluent reason why the observation did not matter.
numbers: Correct 18.07 vs wrong 390.4 (about 21 times too high).
quote: This is an instance of the well-documented phenomenon whereby an LLM produces post hoc rationalisations of erroneous outputs
limits: Exact share of wrong runs is only in a figure, not stated in the text.
agent_relevance: Post hoc rationalisation of an error makes it hard to catch. The agent needs a checker that recomputes, not one that re-reads the explanation.

source: Keppens (2026) An exploratory study of hybrid explanation of Bayesian network derived likelihood ratios
finding: In the Fenton-Neil jury observation (explaining away) network, 4 of 100 runs gave LR about 1.21 instead of the correct 0.66. The prior observation was used in all runs, so it was a propagation error.
limits: Attempts to reproduce the error by editing the network failed, so the cause is unknown.
agent_relevance: Counter-intuitive explaining-away cases are where LLM inference is least reliable. Flag these for symbolic checking.

source: Keppens (2026) An exploratory study of hybrid explanation of Bayesian network derived likelihood ratios
finding: Hybrid prompt: give the model the exact marginals and the LR computed symbolically, and tell it not to recompute. This removed all numeric errors and cut token use and variance.
numbers: 100% correct across all cases over 100 repetitions per network (versus errors above); token counts much lower, mean gap far above the spread.
limits: Prompt told model not to recompute; the model could still misword the meaning.
agent_relevance: A direct template: symbolic engine computes, LLM explains. Matches the schema rule of tool-checked numbers.

source: Keppens (2026) An exploratory study of hybrid explanation of Bayesian network derived likelihood ratios
finding: With marginals only, the model explained the explaining-away case mostly by the marginals and missed the structural reason. Adding partial belief-propagation messages made it describe the explaining-away effect.
numbers: Jury observation LR 0.66. Three prompt modalities compared qualitatively.
limits: Qualitative, no scoring.
agent_relevance: Give the model the flow of influence (message passing), not only end numbers, when the case is counter-intuitive.

source: Keppens (2026) An exploratory study of hybrid explanation of Bayesian network derived likelihood ratios
finding: When probed with a prosecutor-fallacy style restatement, the marginals-supplied model corrected it: the LR is how probable the evidence is under each hypothesis, not the chance of guilt.
numbers: One example exchange; the model answered 'No' and restated the LR as probability of evidence under each hypothesis.
limits: Anecdotal single probe, not a test of fallacy rates.
agent_relevance: Constrained context makes the model resist transposed-conditional errors. Unconstrained rate is not measured here.

source: Qiu et al. (2025/2026) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs fall far short of a normative Bayesian assistant when updating beliefs over five rounds of a flight-recommendation task, and often plateau after one round.
numbers: 624 simulated users, 5 rounds, 100 held-out flight sets per round. Gemma original about 37% in both round 1 and 5. Humans (48 users) improved from round 1 to 5 (p=0.002) but also fell short of Bayes.
limits: Preference learning, not legal evidence. Exact bar values for the larger models were read from a garbled figure.
agent_relevance: LLMs do not accumulate evidence well across turns even when it is simple. Evidence stacking over a long case needs an external ledger.

source: Qiu et al. (2025/2026) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Chain-of-thought, numeric formats, 30 rounds, and base-model variants all failed to fix the weak updating.
numbers: Several appendix ablations (C.1); none gave meaningful improvement.
limits: Tested in this one task family.
agent_relevance: Telling the model to reason more is not a fix for belief updating.

source: Qiu et al. (2025/2026) Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Fine-tuning on a Bayesian assistant's (often wrong) best guesses beat fine-tuning on oracle correct answers and generalised to hotel and web-shopping tasks.
numbers: Three 7-9B models (Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B); Bayesian-tuned predictions agreed with the Bayesian assistant about 80% of the time; all p<0.001; 3 seeds.
limits: Needs training, so it does not apply to our no-training scaffold. Tasks have small hypothesis spaces.
agent_relevance: Shows the skill is learnable, but our agent must instead call an exact Bayes tool.

source: Nafar, Venable, Kordjamshidi (2024) Reasoning over Uncertain Text by Generative Large Language Models
finding: On BLInD (Bayesian networks of up to 10 variables stated in text) plain prompting and chain of thought collapse as the network grows.
numbers: GPT-4 CoT few-shot: 78% at 2 variables, 64% at 3, 36% at 4, 7% at 8 and 9 variables. Llama3 and GPT-3.5 are lower. Basic QA few-shot near 0-3% for all.
limits: Accuracy counted within a tolerance of the right probability; table was read from extracted text, columns may be slightly misaligned; models from 2023-24.
agent_relevance: Hand-computed probability chains fail past a few linked variables.

source: Nafar, Venable, Kordjamshidi (2024) Reasoning over Uncertain Text by Generative Large Language Models
finding: Translating the text to code or a probabilistic program fixes most of this. ProbLog with GPT-4 stays near perfect even for 10 variables.
numbers: GPT-4 ProbLog by network size: 99, 98, 100, 100, 96, 97, 97, 98, 96 percent. GPT-4 Monte Carlo 100 down to 88; PAL (plain Python) 100 down to 7. Llama3 ProbLog 90 down to 78.
limits: Text states clean numbers; real legal evidence has vague, disputed numbers.
agent_relevance: Best match for our agent: write the case as a Bayesian network in a solver, not as prose arithmetic. Pick the solver language with care (PAL failed, ProbLog worked).

source: Nafar, Venable, Kordjamshidi (2024) Reasoning over Uncertain Text by Generative Large Language Models
finding: Sub-tasks (extract numbers, extract graph) were near perfect for strong models: Llama3 and GPT-4 extracted all numbers at 100%, graph generation fell from 99% to about 89-93% on the largest networks.
numbers: Number extraction 100% for GPT-4 and Llama3, above 90% for GPT-3.5; graph generation about 89% at the largest size for Llama3.
limits: Adding sub-task calls to the same prompt sometimes lowered accuracy because the output got longer.
agent_relevance: Split reading the case (LLM) from computing (solver), but check that extraction is correct.

source: Paruchuri et al. (2024) What Are the Odds? Language Models Are Capable of Probabilistic Reasoning
finding: LLMs can estimate percentiles of distributions but are poor at sampling and computing probabilities with no context. Examples in the prompt help a lot.
numbers: Zero-shot percentile error best for uniform (MAE 0.54%) and normal (2.29%). One-shot gains: percentiles +59.14%, sampling +55.26% (K-S), probabilities +70.13%.
limits: Gemini 1.0 Ultra, GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-3.5 Turbo; model-dependent across domains.
agent_relevance: Give worked examples and summary statistics for any numeric step the model must do itself.

source: Paruchuri et al. (2024) What Are the Odds? Language Models Are Capable of Probabilistic Reasoning
finding: Real-world context and a Normal approximation (even a crude one) improved accuracy on average, but not for every distribution.
numbers: Gemini 1.0 Ultra: real-world context plus Normal approximation best on aggregate; exception for resting heart rate. Models appear to interpolate between in-context shots (nearest-neighbour baseline does not).
limits: Idealised distribution tasks, not evidence strength.
agent_relevance: Stating a simple parametric model can help the model reason about spread and tails.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Telling the model to reason as a Bayesian (start with a prior, update on specific information) made forecasts worse across all models.
numbers: Study 1: 38 prompts, 100 ForecastBench questions, four models (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Haiku, GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 405B). Bayesian Reasoning raised Brier score by 0.03 versus control (t about 5.4, p<0.001, still significant after Benjamini-Hochberg).
limits: Questions were general forecasting, not legal. Authors guess at superficial mimicry of Bayesian updating.
agent_relevance: Do not just prompt 'think Bayesian'. A verbal Bayes instruction is not a Bayes computation.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Prompts about base rates helped slightly; 'Base Rate First', 'Frequency-Based Reasoning' and 'Step-Back' beat control in the adjusted analysis for one model.
numbers: Base Rate First mean forecast 0.428; effect about -0.011 to -0.016 Brier (small, negative means better).
limits: Gains were tiny and not robust across all models; Study 2 compound prompts gave no gain.
agent_relevance: Asking for the base rate (reference class) is the one cheap prompt with some support.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Bayesian Reasoning, Propose-Evaluate-Select and chain of thought made forecasts more extreme than control prompts.
numbers: Mean distance from 0.5: 17.2-19.9 percentage points for those prompts versus 11.9-13.4 for control, anti-anchoring and re-reading.
limits: Distance from 0.5 is not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Verbal Bayes prompts push overconfidence. Calibration check needed.

source: He, Qiu, Sap, Shirado (2025) Martingale Score: An Unsupervised Metric for Bayesian Rationality in LLM Reasoning
finding: If a model were a rational Bayesian updater, its revision should not be predictable from its prior belief. LLMs break this: belief entrenchment is widespread, including under chain of thought.
numbers: Positive Martingale Scores in almost all setups; 51 of 54 CoT setups positive. Domains: event forecasting, r/ChangeMyView, OpenReview paper review.
limits: Beliefs read by an LLM judge from the rationale (judge agreement checked across models); no gold standard in value-laden domains.
agent_relevance: Reasoning for longer can lock in the first guess. Our agent should record its prior and test whether it moved only when evidence arrived.

source: He, Qiu, Sap, Shirado (2025) Martingale Score: An Unsupervised Metric for Bayesian Rationality in LLM Reasoning
finding: More entrenchment goes with worse accuracy where truth is known.
numbers: Forecasting CoT: Martingale 0.0 gives Brier below 0.25; Martingale 0.04 gives Brier worse than random guessing (0.25).
limits: Correlation across setups, not a causal test.
agent_relevance: A cheap unsupervised self-check: predictable updates are a red flag.

source: He, Qiu, Sap, Shirado (2025) Martingale Score: An Unsupervised Metric for Bayesian Rationality in LLM Reasoning
finding: A critical-thinking prompt reduced and a prior-conforming prompt increased entrenchment in forecasting, but neither effect was found in ChangeMyView or OpenReview.
numbers: Entrenchment higher in r/ChangeMyView than forecasting for same model and prompt.
limits: Prompt effects not general.
agent_relevance: Prompt wording gives partial control only in domains with checkable outcomes.

source: Araya (2025) Do Chains-of-Thoughts of LLMs Suffer from Hallucinations, Cognitive Biases, or Phobias in Bayesian Reasoning?
finding: Reasoning LLMs solving a cat-and-cards Bayes problem used symbolic probability language and avoided natural frequencies unless told to. One model gave two different answers in two runs.
numbers: Gemini Flash 2.0 gave a correct answer in 255 words and a wrong answer in 389 words in two runs. o3-mini and DeepSeek R1 also tested; 4 prompt variants.
limits: Tiny sample (three models, a few runs), one problem, February 2025. No rates.
agent_relevance: Natural frequency formats (counts out of 1000) help people; the models need an explicit instruction to use them, and even then not reliably.

source: Araya (2025) Do Chains-of-Thoughts of LLMs Suffer from Hallucinations, Cognitive Biases, or Phobias in Bayesian Reasoning?
finding: Prompting for natural frequencies and block pictures changed what the models wrote, but inconsistently. The author calls the persistent symbolic bias a phobia of ecologically valid strategies.
numbers: Qualitative, 3 LLMs; 'whole objects' and 'embodied' prompts incorporated only in part.
limits: Interpretive language. No accuracy table.
agent_relevance: Test natural-frequency rewrites as an operator for the probability step, and measure before relying on it.

source: Jiang et al. (2024) A Peek into Token Bias: Large Language Models Are Not Yet Genuine Reasoners
finding: Conjunction fallacy (Linda-type) items: LLM answers drop when surface tokens change, for example replacing Linda by Bob, or adding a celebrity name. This is evidence of token bias, not rule use.
numbers: Hypothesis tests (McNemar style) on synthetic sets, n=500 for the exemplar-name swap and n=100 for celebrity variants; ten models incl. GPT-4o, Claude 3 Opus, Llama 3 70B. Null of genuine reasoning rejected for almost all.
limits: Synthetic items; effect sizes vary by model.
agent_relevance: Models may pass famous probability puzzles by memory. Test them on re-skinned novel versions, not Linda or taxi.

source: Wong et al. (2023) From Word Models to World Models: Translating from Natural Language to the Probabilistic Language of Thought
finding: Architecture: an LLM (Codex) translates sentences into condition and query statements in a probabilistic program (Church); the engine does the Bayesian inference. In a tug-of-war domain, beliefs update coherently as evidence statements are added.
numbers: Example: estimate that Gabe beats another player at 23.90%; the LLM also maps hedges like 'rarely lazy' to probability values.
limits: Illustrative demonstration, not a benchmark with error rates. The generative model is hand-written.
agent_relevance: Closest published pattern to a legal-evidence agent: LLM reads the testimony, a solver does the posterior.

source: Zhang, Zhang, Kordjamshidi, Cui (2026) Bayesian Network Structure Discovery Using Large Language Models
finding: LLMs can propose the whole graph of a Bayesian network from variable names in one call (PromptBN), and a ReAct-style refinement adds data (ReActBN). Strongest when data is scarce.
numbers: PromptBN exact on Asia (SHD 0), SHD 0.6 on Cancer, best on Insurance (SHD 35.6); ReActBN best on 6 of 9 datasets and 40.2 SHD on Insurance (Table 1).
limits: Benchmarks are textbook networks that may be in training data. Graphs for legal cases are contested.
agent_relevance: An agent could draft a case network, then humans or checks critique it (Fenton-Neil idioms).

source: Guha et al. (2023) LegalBench: A Collaboratively Built Benchmark for Measuring Legal Reasoning in LLMs
finding: The only evidence-law item in this benchmark is the hearsay task (rule application). GPT-4 beats GPT-3.5, mostly on non-verbal hearsay and in-court statements, but still struggles with 'not offered for the truth of the matter'.
numbers: 162 tasks, 20 LLMs from 11 families. Hearsay slice analysis (Table 6), slices small.
limits: Not about probabilities or likelihood ratios. Legal benchmarks do not yet test prosecutor's fallacy or Bayesian weighing.
agent_relevance: Gap: no public benchmark found that tests LLMs on legal Bayesian evidence reasoning. We may need to build one.

source: Leonelli (2026) Beyond Post-hoc Explanation: Toward Glassbox AI via Probabilistic Mediation
finding: Position paper: put a Bayesian network in front of the generative model as an ante-hoc mediation layer so reasoning is auditable and contestable, argued for legal and public-administration use. Illustrated by a benefit eligibility scenario.
numbers: No experiments or error rates. Lists open problems: semantic alignment, dynamic model construction, probabilistic grounding, human governance.
limits: Vision paper; no evidence it works.
agent_relevance: Supports the design but not the performance claims.

source: Cuellar (2025) The Prosecutor's Fallacy and Expert Testimony: A Modern Take Using Likelihood Ratios
finding: Argues that experts should report likelihood ratios, not posterior probabilities of guilt, because posteriors need priors and non-forensic evidence that belong to the fact finder. Notes lay readers find LRs hard.
numbers: Worked on a modified real case; no experiment.
limits: Human-focused. Only abstract and introduction read in detail.
agent_relevance: Output rule for our agent: report the weight of one piece of evidence as an LR with its assumptions; leave the prior to the human.
